findings.description: The EARS text's trigger for the SubCent anomaly is stated only as a property of the RAW reading — "a non-positive numeric price reading (0.0 or negative)". The real code (price_to_cents, sheets-view/src/lib.rs:362-385) instead gates on the ROUNDED CENTS VALUE: `if cents <= 0 { return Err(SubCent) }`, which also catches a genuinely POSITIVE raw reading that rounds down to 0 or fewer cents (e.g. $0.0001) — pinned by the real test `subcent_positive_price_is_degraded_anomaly_not_zero` (tests/marks.rs:73-98). Because the spec enumerates only the raw-value condition, a literal, faithful implementation of the spec text alone (A1) computes `let cents = (raw * 100.0).round() as i64;` with NO post-rounding non-positive check, so for raw=0.0001 it returns `MarkOutcome::Mark(Cents(0))` — a real defect that directly contradicts the spec's own rationale clause ("a bad reading never silently understates... value"): a $0.00 mark for a real, if tiny, position silently zeroes it out. A2 and A3 don't reproduce the bug only because they punt float→Cents conversion out of scope entirely (A2's `Valid(f64)` passthrough; A3's caller-supplied `to_cents` closure assumed 'infallible for positive finite input') — neither of them closes the gap either, they just don't demonstrate it concretely. All 3 B reconstructions (B1 case 3/UB1, B2 UB3, B3 U4) independently pin the exact same extra rule as a rounded-cents-≤0 check distinct from the raw-value check. This is the strongest finding: the same underlying spec incompleteness produces a demonstrable A-side compliance failure AND an independently-pinned B-side extra rule.

The float→Cents rounding algorithm is fully unstated by SHEET-MARK-007 but tightly pinned in code+tests: `round_half_to_even` ("banker's rounding") via `SCALE = 1_000_000` — `numerator = (price_usd * 100.0 * SCALE as f64).round() as i128`, then `pt_core::round_half_to_even(numerator, SCALE)` — with ties resolving to even: `1.005 -> Cents(100)` ($1.00), `1.015 -> Cents(102)` ($1.02), per the real test `usd_price_converts_to_cents_round_half_to_even` (tests/marks.rs:62-71). All 3 B outputs (B1 U1/constants-pinned note, B2 U1/U2, B3 U1) independently reconstruct this exact rule and constant. The 3 A outputs, having no basis in the spec text for any of this, each invent something different — A1 uses plain `f64::round` (round-half-away-from-zero), A2 defers conversion entirely as out of scope, A3 abstracts it behind an injected `to_cents` closure — precisely because nothing in SHEET-MARK-007 constrains the conversion algorithm at all.

A second, independent finiteness guard exists in the real code after the scaling step: `let scaled = price_usd * 100.0 * SCALE as f64; if !scaled.is_finite() { return Err(DegradeReason::Permanent); }` (lib.rs:373-376) — catching arithmetic overflow of the intermediate scaled value even when the raw `price_usd` itself was finite. SHEET-MARK-007's "non-finite reading" language describes the raw reading only; this is a second, implementation-only safety net. All 3 B outputs flag it as a distinct rule (B1 point 6, B2 UB2, B3 U3), while none of the 3 A outputs anticipate an intermediate-overflow case at all — naturally, since nothing in the spec text implies the scaled value needs its own check.

In `read_marks` (lib.rs:848-869), a numeric reading that degrades via `price_to_cents` (either SubCent or Permanent) goes straight to `out.degraded.insert(...)` with NO fallback to a cached prior mark, whereas a `PriceReading::Transient` that stays transient past the poll window (or a `None` reading) explicitly DOES fall back to `prior.get(s)` before degrading. All 3 B outputs call this out as a deliberate, distinct rule (B1 point 9, B2 E1, B3 U6), contrasting it with the Transient/TimedOut carry-forward path. This is the weakest of the four findings: SHEET-MARK-007's "never as a mark" language is plausibly read to already imply this (a bad numeric reading shouldn't resurrect an old mark either), so it may not be a hard contradiction; and per code inspection, no test in tests/marks.rs actually exercises this exact branch with a non-empty `prior` map (subcent_positive_price_is_degraded_anomaly_not_zero and zero_and_negative_price_are_degraded_not_a_zero_or_negative_mark both use `BTreeMap::new()` for prior) — so the rule is structurally present in the code but not verified by any test.

notes:
Read the real implementation (sheets-view/src/lib.rs, price_to_cents at lines 362-385, read_marks at 817-887) and the real test file (tests/marks.rs) directly before comparing against all 6 candidate outputs.

A-direction agreement is high on everything the spec text actually addresses (finite-check-before-non-positive-check ordering, reuse of the EARS's own SubCent/Permanent vocabulary, and enforcing "never as a mark" structurally via separate enum variants) — the only divergence among A1/A2/A3 is on the float->Cents conversion algorithm itself, which all three explicitly flag as unspecified/out-of-scope, and that is exactly where finding #1 originates (A1's naive conversion demonstrates a concrete defect; A2/A3 sidestep by punting).

B-direction agreement is very high — all three B reconstructions independently converge on the same SCALE=1_000_000 constant, the same round_half_to_even algorithm with the same tie examples, the same double-finiteness-guard structure, the same positive-rounds-to-zero SubCent case, and the same no-prior-carry-forward / absence-from-to_ledger_marks semantics, differing mainly in EARS-clause organization/wording rather than substance.

Overall this reads as a case where the EARS text is a compressed, high-level statement of intent ("non-positive raw reading -> SubCent, non-finite raw reading -> Permanent") that is materially under-specified relative to both (a) what a literal implementation needs to actually satisfy the stated rationale (finding #1, BD) and (b) the concrete algorithm/edge-case handling the real code and tests actually pin down (findings #2-#4, B-only).
